vignette:
He is 27, a single African man who spends most days driving a taxi through the city, moving other people from one place to another while keeping large parts of himself sealed off. When he speaks about his childhood, he does not begin with a single incident at first. He begins with the atmosphere in the house: the sound of a chair scraping hard against the floor, the sudden silence that meant his caregiver was in a dangerous mood, the way his own body learned to listen before his mind understood. As a boy, he becomes skilled at reading footsteps in the hallway and the force of a cupboard door shutting. He learns that a misplaced shoe, a poor school result, a spilled cup, or sometimes nothing he can name can lead to being hit.

The abuse is physical and repeated. He remembers being grabbed by the arm so hard it leaves marks, being beaten with a belt, being slapped across the face, being kicked when he is already on the ground. He remembers trying not to cry because crying sometimes makes it worse. He remembers staring at one crack in the wall while waiting for it to end. In those moments, he feels outside himself, as if he is watching a smaller boy being hurt and cannot help him. Afterwards, he goes to school sore and exhausted, careful with the way he sits at his desk. He says little. Teachers describe him as quiet and respectful. At home he is called stubborn, ungrateful, bad.

As he grows older, he becomes constantly alert. He keeps his room in order because disorder feels unsafe. He avoids bringing friends home. When other boys play loudly or shove each other jokingly, he does not experience it as play. His body tightens and his heart begins to race before he can think. At night, he lies awake listening for movement in the house. Sleep comes lightly. Even when he is not being hurt, he is preparing to be hurt. He begins to carry a private conviction that he is always one mistake away from punishment.

By adolescence, he spends more time outside the house whenever he can. He tells himself he is independent, but underneath that is a fierce need never to be trapped again. He works small jobs, saves money, and leaves home as soon as it is possible. Leaving brings relief, but not peace. In rented rooms and shared apartments, he still startles at raised voices. If someone knocks unexpectedly, his chest jolts. He avoids arguments, especially with older men, because the anger in their faces makes him feel suddenly young and defenseless. Relationships do not last long. He wants closeness, but when someone comes to know him too well, he becomes tense and distant. He finds himself scanning for signs that affection might turn into control.

Driving becomes a job that fits and also deepens his way of living. In the taxi, he is alone, in motion, and in charge of his own space. He likes that he can decide who enters, where he looks, when he takes a break. Yet the work keeps him exposed to exactly the kinds of things his nervous system cannot ignore. A passenger slams the door and his whole body jumps. A drunk customer shouting into a phone leaves him gripping the steering wheel so tightly his hands ache. If two men argue on the roadside, he feels his stomach drop and instinctively checks the mirrors, the locks, the quickest route away. He tells himself these are ordinary precautions for a driver, but he knows his reactions are stronger than other people’s. Sometimes after a tense ride, he has to pull over because his breathing becomes shallow and he feels as if something terrible is about to happen.

He does not talk easily about nightmares, but when he does, they are vivid and physical. He wakes sweating, heart pounding, sometimes with the sensation that someone is standing over him. On bad nights, he checks the door repeatedly before trying to sleep again. During the day, memories arrive without warning: the sting of a slap when he sees a parent yank a child’s arm at a taxi rank, the old helplessness when he hears a belt buckle clink, the familiar dread when someone’s tone shifts from calm to sharp. He tries to push these thoughts away, but they return more forcefully. There are days he feels detached from the world, as if he is watching life through glass while still doing what is required—picking up passengers, checking the app, asking for destinations, making change.

What troubles him most in the present is not only fear but shame. He judges himself for being affected by things that happened long ago. He believes he should be stronger by now. At the same time, he notices how much of his life has been organized around avoiding danger, anger, dependence, and exposure. He keeps conversations superficial. He rarely visits anyone’s home. He prefers daytime shifts, though they pay less, because nights leave him too keyed up. He is often tired, often irritable, and almost never fully at ease. Even in moments of calm, some part of him remains braced, listening for the first sign that safety is about to disappear.
